# We have become protectors of English: revisiting policies of publishing in English in non-Anglophone academia
Seyyed-Abdolhamid Mirhosseini <sup>a</sup>, Farnoosh Rashed and Mohsen Shirazizadeh <sup>b</sup>
<sup>a</sup>Faculty of Education, The University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong, Hong Kong; <sup>b</sup>Department of English, Faculty of Literature, Alzahra University, Tehran, Iran
#### **ABSTRACT **
In the vigorous trend of international publication as a crucial research performance indicator, English claims the status of the uncontested global language of academic publishing. In this study, after providing a sketch of the policies of writing and publishing in English in Iran (reflected in national policy documents and university bylaws), we probe the perspectives of nine Iranian higher education policy experts about these policies through semi-structured interviews. The findings reveal that while policy documents indicate strong orientations in favor of publishing in English, the main justifications behind these policies appear to be vague ideas of demonstrating local academic capabilities and winning international reputation. However, the participants admit that ignoring the peculiarities of different academic fields and neglecting real-life research concerns while overemphasizing the number of research products are the main pitfalls of the policies. Their view of these problems and their suggested solutions indicate little consideration of the concern over the dominance of English in the world today. We discuss some aspects of this concern in relation to the neocolonial status of English in non-Anglophone countries where other languages and cultures can be overshadowed by a dominant so-called global academic lingua franca.
#### **ARTICLE HISTORY **
Received 5 August 2023 Accepted 7 December 2023
#### **KEYWORDS **
Publishing in English; dominance of English; academic writing; academic publishing; higher education policy
## Introduction
With the fever of internationalization on the rise in higher education systems, universities around the world increasingly aim their policies at overcoming barriers in the way of obtaining better ranking positions in research productivity, among other criteria (Buckner, 2020; Ekmekci et al., 2018; Jones et al., 2021). Therefore, research performance policies in many places tend to oblige academics to publish in international journals with high impact factors (e.g. AlMubarak, 2020; Flowerdew & Habibie, 2022; Hughes & Bennett, 2013). Within this broad policy trend growing worldwide, the English language is gaining the status of the uncontested dominant language of publishing even in countries where it is not the first or even the second language (Englander & Corcoran, 2019). In Iran, like many non-English speaking countries, international academic
publication in English has become an index of scientific excellence, particularly over the last two decades (Doostdar & Mirhosseini, 2009; Rezaei & Seyri, 2019). This, however, has sparked debates since Persian as the official national language has always been a source of pride for its rich world-famous literature and its traditionally respected status in many parts of Western, Central, and Southern Asia throughout history.
This highlighted role of English as a language of academic publishing has been reflected in the official Iranian higher education policies. Nonetheless, apart from a few limited-scope examinations of such policies and how they are received by Iranian academics (e.g. Mansouri Nejad et al., 2020; Mirhosseini & Shafiee, 2019), there has been no in-depth investigation of official policies of writing and publishing in English in this context. Therefore, in this article, sketching how official policies in Iran encourage faculty members to write and publish in English (Rashed et al., 2023), we draw on interviews with a number of higher education policy experts to understand their perspectives and concerns about overt and covert policies and the actual practices of academic writing and publishing in English by Iranian academics. Examining these policies and expert reflections on them can offer useful insights into the complexities of academic writing and publishing in English as a foreign language in contexts like Iran and the challenges such policies may pose for academics of non-English-speaking background. More fundamentally, the study can address concerns about how policies in higher education systems around the world can perpetuate the continued neocolonial dominance of English in the sphere of knowledge (Durand, 2006; Navarro et al., 2022; Pennycook, 2007; Wright, 2016).
# **Background **
Higher education policies across the world are increasingly influenced by external forces of global ranking and the competitive climate of research and publication (Buckner, 2020; Dan & Fengqiao, 2015; Komotar, 2019; Li, 2016; Yudkevich et al., 2015). The orientation of these policies towards globalization tends to exert different kinds of pressure on university administrators, faculty members, researchers, and even students with regard to the nature and quantity of their teaching, learning, and research (AlMubarak, 2020; Ekmekci et al., 2018; Shahriari & Ghonsooly, 2019). Within this context of intersecting internationalization forces, language-related issues appear to shape a considerable body of concerns in university policies and practices (Soler et al., 2018; Tamtik & Jang, 2018). Debates around the language of instruction in national and international contexts (Agbo & Pak, 2017; Hamid et al., 2013; Hu & Lei, 2014; Selvi, 2014) and language proficiency requirements as part of university admission mechanisms (Bo et al., 2023; Eckes & Althaus, 2020; Pearson, 2021) are some of the prominent language challenges in higher education. Especially significant in this regard is the language of research dissemination which has turned to be a debatable topic for at least two decades (Ammon, 2006; Englander & Corcoran, 2019; Flowerdew & Habibie, 2022; Flowerdew & Li, 2009; Hyland, 2016).
Language can be understood as more than a mere communication tool, and as a social practice intertwined with culture and identity (Forbes & Rutgers, 2021; Jamshidi & Rezaei, 2020; Kramsch, 1998). The language of research publication highlighted in national and institutional policies in different contexts can play a crucial role within
the contestations related to this social practice, which can create both opportunities and challenges for scholars' professional life and their identities as researchers, and this has been the subject of relatively extensive debates (e.g. Cho & Yi, 2018; Dan & Fengqiao, 2015; Xu & Ou, 2022). Within this ongoing discussion, the status of English as the language of research publication has been a key concern (e.g. Bardi, 2015; Englander & Corcoran, 2019; Liu & Buckingham, 2022; Thomas & Reinersten, 2019). To enhance research productivity and gain recognition in the wider academic world, reporting research outcomes and publishing them in prestigious journals with higher publication visibility mediated through international indexes (predominantly in English) have become a global trend (Ekmekci et al., 2018; Gill, 2006; Jones et al., 2021; Kuteeva et al., 2020). Aimed at meeting an international standard, higher education policies can switch the focus from fulfilling local needs to addressing global hot topics raised in reputable (English-medium) journals (Kennedy, 2011; Quinn, 2018; Sandy & Shen, 2019).
Similar to many other contexts (e.g. Bocanegra-Valle, 2014; Davis, 2019; Gill, 2006; Lee & Lee, 2013; Muresan & Pérez-Llantada, 2014; Zheng & Guo, 2019), official higher education policies in Iran have made scholars competitively involved in the global trend of academic writing and publishing in English (Arani et al., 2018; Atai et al., 2018). These official policies do pronounce Persian as a symbol of national unity among different linguistic groups, a language of rich literature and recognized literary figures, and as a traditional language of knowledge and scholarship in an important area of the world (Davari-Ardakani & Ahmadipour, 2009; Ghamari & Hassanzadeh, 2010). Nonetheless, the policies and practices in Iran seem to have been influenced by the ranking systems and the global push to publish in English (Rezaei & Seyri, 2019). They encourage English language publishing as a prerequisite of recruitment, academic and professional promotion, and research funding (Doostdar & Mirhosseini, 2008; Mirhosseini & Shafiee, 2019). Therefore, despite the emphasis in higher order national policies, Persian appears to be marginalized as a language of academic publication.
Since the establishment of modern universities in Iran around 90 years ago, higher education has acted as a significant part of the social and political sphere in addition to its knowledge-related functions. Since then, higher education has evolved into a centralized national system that nowadays governs even private universities at the policy level, despite their relative autonomy at the administrative level (Farasatkhah et al., 2008; Rajaee, 2023). As a significant aspect of the national level higher education policies, the language of instruction at all levels in Iran is Persian as the official national language, and there is no English-medium instruction except for students majoring in English. High-stakes tests, various exams, theses, conference presentations, and most local journals are also in Persian. However, touched by globalization trends (Malekinia et al., 2019), during the past two decades, the two Iranian ministries in charge of science and research, namely the Ministry of Science, Research, and Technology, and the Ministry of Health and Medical Education have moved towards models of 'research universities', which embrace international ranking systems and put emphasis on international (English language) publication (Doostdar & Mirhosseini, 2009; Malekinia et al., 2019; Rezaei & Seyri, 2019).
Although the issue of writing and publishing in English has been empirically explored from linguistic perspectives in various contexts (e.g. Bocanegra-Valle, 2014; Flowerdew,
2008; Hanauer & Englander, 2011; Politzer-Ahlesa et al., 2016; Zheng & Guo, 2019), it appears not to be adequately examined from a policy perspective, and has not been extensively discussed in the context of Iran. One of the few studies investigating this topic in Iran has addressed policies that set the ground for the trend of publishing research articles in English in an Iranian medical university (Mirhosseini & Shafiee, 2019). It was argued that the official policies in that context emphasize research publication as perhaps the most important criterion for academic promotion since higher scores are given to publishing in internationally-indexed journals. Related concerns were addressed in an investigation of Iranian doctoral students' motives, hurdles, and strategies in academic writing and publishing (Rezaei & Seyri, 2019). Similarly, a study on international English-medium publication by Iranian doctoral students of Humanities and Social Sciences, revealed their desire to publish in English despite practical challenges (Mansouri Nejad et al., 2020).
Considering this background of research and discussions, there are significant unexplored policy considerations in this regard in different non-Anglophone contexts, including Iran. Specifically, Iranian official national and university-level higher education policy documents which include regulations on research dissemination still invite further scrutiny. Therefore, this research can not only shed light on some unexamined problems in this area by probing policies of writing and publishing in English as a foreign language in the Iranian centralized higher education system, but can also act as an invitation for further discussions of policy matters in other higher education contexts. A consideration of the overt policies reflected in official documents and eliciting the perspectives of policy experts in this regard can reveal some of the standpoints behind these policies as well as the challenges and possible paths of transformation in the Iranian higher education system and beyond.
# Methodology
This study is part of a large-scale project in which a considerable body of official higher education policy documents in Iran and the perspectives of different groups of participants were explored. In what we present in this article, after sketching the major policy orientations with regard to writing and publishing in English in official higher education policy documents in Iran, we focus on the perspectives of a number of policy experts about these orientations. Our first major data set in the main large-scale study, which was to depict officially stated policy directions, included a bulk of 30 national policy documents (about 500 pages) produced within the past two and a half decades along with 170 university bylaws released by 46 reputable state universities all over the country during the same period (about 1500 pages).
The other body of data was collected through semi-structured interviews with different stakeholders including nine higher education policy experts some of whom used to be policy makers themselves. One of them is a former high-ranking government official and the president of a major non-government university; four are current or former members of recruitment and promotion committees in leading universities in Iran; two are faculty members with former high-ranking administrative roles in major universities in Tehran; and two are scholars specifically researching policies of higher education, science, and technology. The interviews were aimed at eliciting these policy
experts' ideas about the role that English plays in Iranian academia; justifications they see for the current policies of research writing and publishing; the challenges that may rise due to the current regulations related to writing and publishing (in English) for faculty members across disciplines; and possible alternatives and solutions that they may be able to propose in this regard. Individual interviews were conducted in Persian and varied in length between 40-70 minutes each (overall, around nine hours) and were recorded and later transcribed and translated.
To analyze the body of documents, qualitative content analysis was employed which emphasizes identifying, analyzing, and interpreting themes or patterns of meaning within the data to create insightful, rich, and trustworthy research findings (Mayring, 2014; Roller, 2019). On this basis, the policy documents were coded in several rounds. They were read in search of codes relevant to the research issue and were then re-read multiple times to specify specific thematic categories based on initial codes. The themes were later polished to clarify the relationships among them, and the most notable examples were then selected to illustrate each category. The analytical approach to the bodies of data collected through interviews is based on a grounded theoryperspective (Charmaz, 2014). The interview transcripts were coded based on open, focused, and axialcoding procedures (Mirhosseini, 2020). The interconnections among them were then considered in a theoretical coding process. The findings from documents and interviews were then integrated to present an overall image of the policies and practices of writing and publishing in Iranian universities.
# **Findings **
Qualitative content analysis of policy documents revealed four major categories of policies regarding writing and publishing in English in Iranian universities. An overview of these policy lines is presented along with some data excerpts in the Documents section below. A detailed illustration and discussion of these overt policy directions embedded in national and university level documents has been provided in anotherreport of a part of this large-scale project specifically focusing on these documents (Rashed et al., 2023). The interview findings reflecting the perspectives of policy experts participating in this research are then presented as the main body of findings in this article in three categories under the Interviews section. Their views are elaborated through detailed explanations and ample examples quoted from verbatim interview transcripts. All italic parts in the following sections are quotes excerpted from the texts of the documents.
#### **Documents **
Our exploration of the documents revealed four main categories of forces that push Iranian academics to publish in English. The findings indicate that (1) higher scores are assigned to articles published in English (compared to those in Persian) in all kinds of research assessment (This is briefly presented below under *Double Score*); (2) more financial incentives and cash rewards are received by research products written in English (Financially Rewarded); (3) there are clear obligations in this regard since the policies explicitly exert administrative forces to oblige faculty members to write in
internationally-indexed journals, which practically means writing in English rather than Persian (To Be Employed); and (4) the policies tend to persuade academic staff that writing in English wins them more recognition and prestige (Outstanding Researcher). These four categories are briefly presented and exemplified below.
# 'Double score'
Based on the documents, in evaluating research activities, higher scores are assigned to research products published in English compared to those in Persian. For instance, in a nationally leading university, papers published by JCR/Q1 journals receive 10.5 points while the ones published by other journals can receive as low as 3 points. The same difference can be found in several university regulations, allocating more scores to international (English language) publications than local ones. This is not limited to journal articles, as faculty members also gain higher points by writing books, book chapters, and conference papers in international outlets (in English). Based on the list of international publishers provided by one of the major universities, books published by international publishers [i.e. in English] receive 15 points while those published by national publishers gain 10 points. As for conferences, full papers published in the proceedings of international conferences gain 2 points whereas those published in national conferences receive 1 point. In brief, the policy indicates that to gain the highest scores, faculty members should write their research outcomes in English in order to be able to publish them in international venues.
# 'Financially rewarded'
Some research activities can bring financial incentives such as cash bonuses, grants, and incentive salary bases. Most of the documents state that papers published in journals indexed by JCR and WOS will be financially rewarded. One of the leading universities, for example, gives the highest amount of money that is 500 million Rials to papers published in Science and Nature. In another bylaw, the bonus for papers published in ISI journals will be up to 5 times more than that of papers published in other journals. As for grants, the highest amount awarded by a well-known university is 100 million Rials for papers published in journals indexed by JCR and up to 60 million Rials for papers published in other journals. According to bylaws of several universities, faculty members can enjoy incentive salary bases by gaining certain scores out of publishing papers in journals indexed by JCR/Q1 and Q2, Scopus/Q1 and Q2. Overall, almost all kinds of financial rewards are set at higher bands for publications in JCR and Scopus indexed (i.e. English language) journals.
# 'To be employed'
The documents show that (prospective) faculty members have to meet certain requirements related to English language publication as prerequisites of recruitment, tenure, and promotion. To be recruited in some universities, among other requirements, applicants should have at least … 5 papers published in internationally indexed journals. For tenure, an example of the requirements is at least two papers
published by international journals, one of which must be JCR/Q1 for associate professors and JCR/Q2 for assistant professors. Based on another bylaw, to be promoted, applicants should obtain at least 9 out of the 15 required points as an outcome of writing papers published in international journals. Therefore, a minimum number of papers published in international (English language) journals are set as obligatory for recruitment, tenure, and promotion.
# 'Outstanding researcher'
In addition to employment by reputable universities, the recognition and reputation that faculty members can enjoy at different stages of their career is another aspect of writing and publishing in English. As an example, according to the related bylaws, to be nominated for the specific title of 'Outstanding Researcher', 20 points should be gained from research activities out of which at least 15 points are related to ISI papers. In the major administrative practice of selecting 'Distinguished Professors', as another instance, they should gather enough points out of writing 50 papers published in journals indexed by JCR/Q1. Moreover, based on one of the university bylaws, to take sabbaticals for the second time as a full professor, at least 5 papers published in leading international journals are required. The prestige that comes with these titles seems to be a significant encouragement for faculty members to publish in internationally-indexed journals, that is, those in English.
The four emerging patterns of policy directions in the examined documents can be interpreted in light of the broad orientations of internationalization – cum Englishization – of higher education discussed, among others, by de Wit and Altbach [(2021](#page-15-16)) and contributors to the volume edited by Wilkinson and Gabriels ([2021](#page-19-4)). In addition to throwing national and local languages to the margins of academic publishing (Englander & Corcoran, [2019](#page-16-3); Liu & Buckingham, [2022)](#page-17-7), this may be interpreted as a systematic transition to celebrating what we have elsewhere called 'empty publication; that is producing publishable texts with little or no research basis' (Rashed et al., [2023,](#page-18-1) p. 78). Reifying the concerns of some of the existing discussions that we referred to in the Background section above about a climate of competition over writing for publication in English in Iran and beyond (Atai et al., [2018](#page-15-12); Davis, [2019;](#page-15-10) Zheng & Guo, [2019](#page-19-3)), the policies set by these documents appear to bluntly aim at managing local scholarly resources along the paths dictated by globalization mechanisms.
# Interviews
Apart from the document findings sketched above, the main findings presented in this article are based on interviews that elicited policy experts' perspectives on the official policies of research writing and publishing in Iranian academia and their opinions on the English–Persian interface in this regard. The analysis of the interviews revealed three major aspects of participants' perspectives and positions vis-a-vis the existing policies: (1) their Justifications for the attitudes, expectations, and policy setting processes that have led to the current policies; (2) the Problems that they observe in these policies and the challenges that they can create for higher education, science, and technology at the national level; and (3) the Remedies that these experts can suggest for the
higher education system and faculty members across disciplines to overcome the related difficulties. In the following three sections, these findings are presented and exemplified by interview data extracts. Referring to the nine participants, PE stands for Policy Expert. All italic parts are quotes from translated interview transcripts.
#### **Justifications **
The interviewed policy experts elaborated on some of the possible justifications behind the policies specified in the official documents and university bylaws about English writing and publishing. As an instance, to PE1, informing others of the outcome of their studies is among the main responsibilities of faculty members. In his view, the dissemination of these outcomes cannot be confined to Iran and should be published internationally to be judged in the best possible way. In this respect, PE2 pointed out that international indexing is significant because it is a mechanism of implementing strict rules for evaluating research outcomes. To him, the number of citations is also significant as it shows how useful research results have been for the whole world. The participants seem to perceive the need for international knowledge dissemination and the related mechanisms of peer review as the most prominent justification for the push to publish internationally. The followings are quotes from other participants referring to the quality of international (English language) journals:
- Publishing papers in ISI journals proves faculty members' level of knowledge. This is so important ... (PE3) - Publishing more quality papers in internationally-indexed journals facilitates overcoming the challenges for recruitment and promotion processes, especially if applicants are intended to apply for top universities ... (PE4)
PE1 believed that writing and publishing papers is one of the main responsibilities of faculty members: They should make themselves known to others in international academic circles, communicate with scholars in other countries, and demonstrate their knowledge in the form of journal papers. Supporting the same perspective, PE2 and PE3 maintained that international indexing and quartiles show the value and quality of major international journals. The participants generally endorsed the idea that to remain competitive in the international academic arena, scholars need to be innovative and write high quality journal papers which are frequently cited. As seen in the first of the following two quotes, in their view, this justifies the significant role that writing and publishing in English plays in recruitment and promotion and, as noted in the second quote, international cooperation and communication is also at stake:
- ... faculty members with higher numbers of papers written in English will pass through these processes easily because they can help the university be more competitive internationally. (PE4) - The reason behind the emphasis on writing journal papers in English is active cooperation among scholars in international academia. Faculty members in their field should discuss issues with others in their discipline in order to contribute to the whole field. (PE3)
More fundamentally, equating high impact (English language) publication with high quality research, PE5 and PE7 observed that since papers written in English enjoy higher quality and are known as the primary criterion for scientific development in the world, they are given higher scores. To them, Iranian scholars should follow the same path to gain international reputation, prove their abilities, and expand their knowledge. PE6 and PE8 held that papers published in national journals in Iran are not that much valuable. PE9 also indicated that since Iran is among developing countries ... and lacks enough facilities for doing quality projects, Iranian scholars must write their research outcomes in English to attract investment. Overall, these experts found the existing policies justifiable on the ground that writing and publishing in English is more beneficial in different ways for the country compared to reporting research outcomes in Persian and publishing them in national journals.
The justifications for the policies of pushing for publishing in English in this context significantly align with the mainstream logic of relying on English as a means of success and this tends to shrug off the debates on the sociopolitics of English and its dominance (Pennycook, 2007; Phillipson, 1992). The offered justifications for the publication policies in strong favor of English significantly include the idea that we need to disseminate the bodies of knowledge that our universities and researchers create - and English is 'the default language' for such a purpose (Bocanegra-Valle, 2014; Kirilova et al., 2023). This assumption is fueled by the existing dominance of English, but also importantly further fuels this dominance. Such assumptions may be interpreted as either the policy makers' unawareness of, or their lack of sensitivity to the colonial history and neocolonial politics of English in academia, among other domains (Navarro et al., 2022; Wright, 2016). However, the policy making arena in this regard appears to be more complicated, as reflected in the participants' opinions on the pitfalls of such policies in the next section.
## **Problems **
Despite the fact that the participants explained some of the reasons behind the adopted policies, they did acknowledge that the policies have given rise to various problems. For example, PE2 argued that these policies have taken the nature of academic disciplines for granted: For faculty members in some majors, particularly in Humanities and Social Sciences, writing in English is very demanding. In line with the same perspective, PE7 thought that issues discussed in these disciplinary areas vary considerably based on geography, language, culture, and religion. He argued that many local and discipline-specific concepts cannot not be transfered interculturally through translation and are thus prone to misunderstanding by people from other countries and cultures. Comparing the nature of fields across disciplines, PE9 stated that it is not reasonable to expect faculty members in Humanities and Social Sciences to write and publish as many papers in English as academics in Chemistry. His reason was that elaborating concepts in these soft disciplines is time-consuming, unlike issues in Engineering and Basic sciences which in most cases do not need to be culturally interpreted. PE4 and PE6 expressed related concerns from similar standpoints:
• How can we oblige all faculty members to write papers only in English? For instance, those who are experts in Islamic Mysticism should definitely write papers in the language which is understandable for the Islamic world. (PE4)
. When all concepts in Humanities and Social Sciences are directly connected to philosophy, ways of thinking, and mentalities, it is obvious that a large number of our papers are rejected … It does not mean that they are low quality papers. The main reason is that international journals' editorial boards are not aware of what goes on in our country, don't know about our culture, and are not aware of the problems we try to address. (PE6)
To these policy experts, obliging academics in all fields to report their research outcomes mainly in English and publish them in international journals sounded unfair. Still, they admited, the existing policies do exert their forces and reduce the attractiveness of writing in Persian and other languages: Owing to the low scores assigned to papers written in Persian, faculty members prefer not to waste their time and effort on writing their research outcomes in Persian (PE8). An actual example provided by PE1 was that even if you spend years to write a significant research paper on 'Shahname' (a wellknown masterpiece in Persian literature) in Persian, it only gains two points. To him, the value of such literary research work cannot be evaluated through scores and based on the mere criterion of being written in English. He observed that, as a reaction to this policy atmosphere, faculty members in these fields may want to basically abandon writing good research works.
To deal with the challenges of writing in English, PE5 believed, faculty members have thought of tricks which function as shortcuts to bypass the tough requirements. He argued that considering the demanding recruitment and promotion processes which give higher credence to international English language journals, applicants need to publish papers in order not to lose the game. However, since they are not concentrated enough to produce quality English papers and should cope with the difficulties, they prefer … translating their own papers originally written in Persian into English to gain the required scores (PE5). To this policy expert, the final result of such obligations is the mass production of poor quality papers. Here is another similar reflection:
. The aim behind writing papers should be expanding our knowledge not writing the research results in English and publishing them in internationally-indexed journals. Every year, the English papers published by faculty members are listed and counted; the more, the better. Academics get higher prestige, higher ranks, more money, and are finally promoted … [but] they do not make any contribution to academia. (PE1)
Raising the same concern, PE9 argued that because of the current policies, faculty members have to neglect their real research concerns: They are just producing texts in English and do not care about the issues their colleagues in the world are dealing with. The major reason, he believed, is that when it comes to evaluating research dissemination, the focus is on whether they appear in international journals (in English) or not. PE5 also pointed out that because of these tough regulations and many other distractions, a majority of faculty members may not keep themselves up-to-date and find about recent theories in their field. Hence, in his view, the large number of papers written in English by Iranian faculty members cannot help them gain international academic recognition. Therefore, as another participant noted, the problem in a nutshell is that we have
become the protectors of English and we are neglecting our rich language, culture, and history (PE8).
As discussed in the previous section, although the politics of English and its ongoing spread appear not to be a concern of Iranian policy makers, at least in the specific realm of academic writing and publishing, the participants do view different types of pitfalls in these policy directions. The three highlighted problems appear to be the publishing requirements of different fields, the research needs of the society, and emphasis on quantitative increase of publications, which do not explicitly question the dominance of English in this domain (Durand, 2006; Wright, 2016). Similar to other contexts, the policy experts' understandings of these problems and their concern about the policies are mostly about the practical challenges of non-English-speaking academic writers and their attainments (e.g. Luo & Hyland, 2019; Muresan & Pérez-Llantada, 2014; Zheng & Guo, 2019). However, as indicated by the reference to 'protecting English' and the 'neglect of our culture', some of the participants do tend to problematize the policies from the perspective of the dominance of English and its consequences (Ergin & Alkan, 2019; Pennycook, 2007).
#### Remedies
Along with their elaborations on the justifications for current policies and the ensuing problems, the participants proposd some solutions as well. For instance, PE1 thought that we must not perceive all fields via the same lens. It was also argued that faculty members in different disciplines should be evaluated in different ways, and the priority in spending the budget of the country should be given to solving our problems and boosting the quality of our knowledge in all fields not just producing papers in English (PE8). According to PE2, in such a climate, academics themselves can decide in which language they prefer to report their research outcomes. Here are a few more reflections on possible trajectories of mitigating strict emphasis on writing and publishing in English:
- While evaluating scholars in fields like Medicine and Chemistry based on their published papers in internationally-indexed journals is reasonable, it might not be appropriate in other fields such as Arts, considering their nature. Instead, conducting useful projects and creating valuable artworks or inventions can be taken into account in these areas. (PE5) - ... the average number of papers necessary to be written in English by faculty members can be determined more logically. For example, by taking a look at the usual trend of writing and publishing papers in English in Humanities and Social Sciences, authorities can come up with a rough number which can help them set more reasonable regulations in this regard. They won't be compared with other fields in terms of writing English papers anymore. (PE8)
In the view of PE3 and PE9, another possible betterment may come from allocating the same points to papers written in English and Persian if they are of equal quality, regardless of the place of publication. Then, it was argued that in addition to papers written in Persian which are beneficial for addressing our country's problems, we need papers written in English since they can help us show our knowledge to the whole world
(PE7). Moreover, launching more specialized academic journals in each field of study in our own country was noted by one participant as a source of encouragement for scholars to write in Persian (PE1). He thought that writing in English will then be better justified and will be done when it is truly needed. This can ideally improve the meaningfulness of writing in English as well, since rather than a blind push for writing, universities can teach academics how to write quality papers in English (PE1).
Moreover, the participants put emphasis on the importance of specifying different roles for different people in academia: All seem to have only one major goal, which is doing research and reporting the results as journal papers in English (PE4). Nonetheless, some participants suggested that ideally, certain groups of academics can be tasked with writing and publishing in English for whatever advantages it might have; a fish cannot climb a tree (PE6). In the view of PE8 and PE9, by defining the aims behind writing journal papers, we may more meaningfully think about the language in which they should be written. They believed if Iranian scholars write papers for educational purposes and want to solve our problems, they should write in Persian but at the same time writing in English can have its own share of what they do to communicate with the world.
As shown in the previous section, in assessing the problems with the investigated policies, the participants appeared to be mostly obsessed with faculty members' general research challenges and their publishing opportunities and abilities. They showed little explicit concern about questions of the ideological and sociopolitical status of English in this regard (e.g. Ergin & Alkan, 2019; Muresan & Pérez-Llantada, 2014). However, the remedies that they think of may be indirectly related to encountering English as the primary language of publication, as they suggest less focus on writing in English, addressing local research issues, and publishing in local journals. These suggestions highlight the provision of alternative publication spaces that potentially support a climate of translanguaging and knowledge decentring (Bojsen et al., 2023), although this may not necessarily tackle the so-called 'international' publication arena dominated by English (Ives, 2015; Navarro et al., 2022; Wright, 2016).
#### Discussion and conclusion
The interviewed policy experts reflected on conceivable justifications for Iranian policies of academic publishing in English and discussed some ramifications of such policies and possible remedies. To our participants, the main justification for the push to publish in English is that disseminating knowledge and demonstrating academic capabilities in today's world can primarily happen through writing and publishing in English rather than any other language. They also observe that joining the international trend in this regard is a prerequisite of attracting investment and winning international reputation. However, they acknowledge that ignoring the peculiarities of different academic fields, neglecting real-life research concerns, and prioritizing the number of research products in English instead of increasing the quality of teaching and solving actual problems are some of the major pitfalls of these dominant policies. As for encountering these challenges, these policy experts suggest reduced emphasis on journal papers in English, drawing researchers' attention to local research needs by reorienting policies for more balance in favor of writing and publishing in Persian, and founding high ranking international Persian language journals.
The findings of the current study tie well with previous studies despite some discrepancies in the contextual nuances of the examined policies and perspectives. An example is the research conducted by Duszak and Lewkowicz (2008) which argued that Polish academics feel a tension between becoming recognized in the wider academic world and the need to publish in Polish. Flowerdew and Li (2009) and Bocanegra-Valle (2014) also raised related concerns about the trend of domination and hegemony of English as the so-called academic lingua franca in the fields of Humanities and Social Sciences in China, and the hegemony of English for scholarly publishing in multilingual Europe. More recently, AlMubarak's (2020) study on scholars' perspectives about academic writing processes and policies at a Saudi university revealed that faculty members' research autonomy is limited as a result of these policies and that the policies have various consequences for faculty members depending on their nationality. With similar concerns and supporting the findings of the current study, Atai et al. (2018), Rezaei and Seyri (2019), and Mansouri Nejad et al. (2020) showed that Iranian doctoral students publish papers in English to prepare a competition-winning resume, fulfill their course requirements, gain international recognition, and receive expert feedback from professional reviewers.
An important consideration in interpreting the findings of these studies and the positions of policy experts in our study is the specific higher education internationalization view that has focused on the dominance of the English language worldwide (Buckner, 2020; Huang, 2015; Jones et al., 2021). The dominance of English in academic publishing is by some accounts viewed as the result of complex and multifaceted processes shaped by social actions, ideologies, and the resources available to those who wish to publish (Durand, 2006; Duszak & Lewkowicz, 2008; Navarro et al., 2022). To some scholars, this global position of English has its origins in the colonial and neo-colonial contexts (Ergin & Alkan, 2019; Nguyen et al., 2009; Pennycook, 1998). Therefore, the link between the power of English and colonialism is to be understood by examining the discursive effects of colonialism on nations, such as creating images of the Self and the Other (English native speakers and its learners) (Lowe & Pinner, 2016; Pennycook, 2007; Tamimi Sa'd, 2018). When English is perceived as a key to success in trade, science, technology, culture, and education, it may be claimed that the language is interlinked with the continuing neo-colonial patterns of global inequality (Ives, 2015; Phillipson, 1992).
Significantly, the views of policy experts reflected in this study only marginally addresses this wider sociolinguistic aspect of publishing in English as they zoom in on academic processes. Nonetheless, the dominance of English in this realm could be viewed as a continuation of the colonial spread of English that can increasingly overshadow other languages and cultures (Flowerdew, 2008; Lai, 2021; Muresan & Pérez-Llantada, 2014). It arguably correlates with political and economic domination and thus maintains inequitable global cultural and power relationships (Bhambra, 2020; Pennycook, 2007). According to Wright (2016), a language spreads if it is a prerequisite for accessing science and technology, while it is linked to strong ideologies. She believes that given the current status of English, to gain access to the scientific community of communication and achieve international recognition, 'the less powerful in the linguistic equation' have to pay costs: 'as new scientists accepted that they would read and publish in English, it became increasingly difficult for any other group or individual to do otherwise and resist the hegemony' (p. 173). While English enjoys the position of the lingua
franca of twenty-first century academia without serious competition, the historical dynamics that turned English into the dominant language worldwide are already joined by international academic writing and publishing (Durand, 2006; Hamel, 2007; Navarro et al., 2022; Soler, 2019). Academics may, therefore, find it a taken-forgranted part of their profession to fuel the already strong Englishization of universities in the non-English-speaking world (Kirkpatrick, 2011; Thomas & Reinersten, 2019; Wilkinson & Gabriels, 2021).
While we have cast our lens on this ideologically loaded role of English writing and publishing in the Iranian higher education system, the messages of our findings for academics and policymakers in different non-English-speaking contexts across the globe are significant. Our findings may go some way in informing different stakeholders of the reasons behind overt and covert policies in this regard, the challenges they can create, and the need for in-depth views of possible alternatives. Although the dominance of English in the world today is undeniable, reflecting on concerns like the ones we have raised here may also be perceived as part of the engagements of those involved in higher education policy setting/studies as well as academics and researchers in English language education. In order for academics not to function as part of the machinery of the neocolonial dominance of English and as mere protectors of English (in the words of our participant), policy makers may need to pay more focused attention to the importance of critical language awareness and the potential challenges that can be posed to the status of local languages and cultures in the shade of a dominant socalled global academic lingua franca.
